findings.text: The first paragraph clearly says what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. A newcomer can say what this is after one paragraph.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The title and heading name firstmate, a different project, not Athena. A newcomer who arrives at Athena's home page cannot tell at first whether the page is about Athena, about firstmate, or both. The third lede paragraph is what finally explains it.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> / h1 of the same text

findings.text: The first section after the navigation is an error message. It sits where the page should show Athena's main promise: a commit you can trace to the models, the cost and the verdict. The newcomer never sees that promise kept, which weakens the case for why Athena matters.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: This link in the header is meant for the project owner, not a first-time visitor. Nothing says who counts as the owner, so a newcomer may wonder whether it applies to them.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Most of the page covers firstmate's internals in detail: exit codes, lock behaviour and teardown edge cases. A newcomer to Athena has no reason to care about these. The page works as proof that Athena can explain a project, but it is far longer than a first visit needs. The core/expert toggle helps only a little.
findings.source: Sections "Counters", "Transitions", and claims such as "the spawn exits 75 and the item stays queued"

findings.text: The next steps are concrete and in order: clone, check prerequisites, run setup, then a one-line first command, with a note that it acts on the current repository. A newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: Next steps: "Get the code: git clone https://github.com/doodla/athena.git" ... "Install Athena from the checkout: ./setup.sh" ... "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The list mentions cargo but does not list Rust or cargo as a prerequisite, and does not say whether setup.sh installs them. A newcomer without Rust may not know whether they need to install it first.
findings.source: Prerequisites: "a C linker (cc), which cargo needs to build Athena"

findings.text: Several glossary entries say only that the term is undefined. That is honest, but it leaves a newcomer without a working meaning for words the page keeps using.
findings.source: Glossary: "The firstmate source does not define a captain call." / "The firstmate source does not define a heartbeat."

findings.text: This section mentions a studies/ folder without a link and without naming which repository it is in. A newcomer cannot follow it.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
